name: WAVM (libsodium WebAssembly runtime benchmark, 2021-Q1)
baseline: wasmer (LLVM, Cranelift and singlepass backends), wasmtime, V8 (Node.js), lucet, Second State VM
workload: libsodium 1.0.18-stable built-in benchmark suite (cryptographic primitives and codecs) compiled to WASI wasm, the same pre-optimized .wasm run on every runtime; macOS and Linux x86_64 rounds.
claimed_speedup: 'WAVM remains the fastest WebAssembly runtime, beating the competition in every single test.' 'WAVM was still about 15% faster than wasmer' (LLVM backend); on the Linux/x86_64 LLVM round 'wavm remains undethroned' with SSVM coming 'really close'. Results are shown as PNG charts and raw files in 2021-Q1/output, no numeric table in the README.
compiler_and_flags: libsodium ./dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench; system compiler LLVM 11.1.0 (Homebrew) with default optimization flags, output pre-optimized with wasm-opt -O4; runtimes compiled from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode (Node.js stock package); wasm and native builds used the same default flags.
hardware: Intel CPU on macOS and a separate Linux/x86_64 machine; CPU models not stated (an ARM-based CPU was used for a separate aarch64 round that excluded WAVM)
stars_or_usage: 2.8k stars; benchmark repo jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks has 81 stars and was archived on 2026-08-19
tradeoffs: LLVM-based, so compile times are long (the EOS VM README calls WAVM's compilation times 'extremely long and unpredictable'). WAVM does not ship pre-compiled binaries for aarch64, so the author could not benchmark it on ARM; it was therefore not tested on ARM in this suite.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project. Numbers are from February 2021 runtime snapshots and are stale; CPU model is not stated and individual tables are only PNG charts or output files; one author ran the suite. A later 2022-12 round exists in the same repo but its folder holds only pics/res/wasm directories and was not read. Newer 2026 runs of the same suite by the same author were seen only as search snippets (not opened), so they are not cited here.

name: wasm3 (libsodium WebAssembly runtime benchmark, 2021-Q1)
baseline: WAMR (Intel wasm-micro-runtime iwasm) in 'fast interpreter' mode
workload: libsodium 1.0.18-stable built-in benchmark suite compiled to WASI wasm (same .wasm for all runtimes), interpreter round on macOS (Intel) plus an aarch64 round.
claimed_speedup: 'wamr was slower than wasm3 on every single test.' Native code is 'about 30 times faster than wasm3' versus 'about 46 times faster' than wamr; on aarch64 wasm3 runs at 'about 3% of native speed'. Charts only, no numeric table in the README.
compiler_and_flags: libsodium ./dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench; LLVM 11.1.0 with default optimization flags, output pre-optimized with wasm-opt -O4; runtimes built from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode.
hardware: Intel CPU on macOS (model not stated); an ARM-based CPU for the aarch64 round (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Interpreter, so roughly 30x slower than native on this suite and far behind JIT/AOT runtimes; very small footprint (the benchmark author cites about 64Kb code and about 10Kb RAM). The README says wasm3 is entering a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project. February 2021 snapshot: WAMR's fast interpreter was brand new then and has since been reworked, and wasm3 has changed too. CPU models not stated, results are PNG charts, single author. Only WAMR's interpreter mode was tested (not its AOT or JIT).

name: wasm3 (App-Store-eligible interpreter comparison, rebeckerspecialties/wasm-benchmark, 2026-09-22)
baseline: WAMR fast interpreter and wasmtime Pulley interpreter (also the WasmEdge interpreter)
workload: CPU time per call over 17 cases every runtime runs (fib, sieve, crc32, matmul, convolution, audio DSP, bulk memory, call_indirect and vtable dispatch, xmrsplayer tracker, AssemblyScript graphql validation), N=10 reps per platform, interpreter-only builds.
claimed_speedup: Geomean CPU time relative to the fastest runtime: M4 Max E-cores wasm3 1.01, WAMR 1.63, Pulley 2.09, WasmEdge 8.42; iPhone XS E-cores wasm3 1.04, WAMR 1.38, Pulley 1.68, WasmEdge 9.28. On M4 call_indirect CPU ms per call: wasm3 11.67, WAMR 18.48, Pulley 31.53, WasmEdge 84.91. About 1.6x faster than WAMR fast-interp and 2.1x faster than Pulley on the M4, about 1.3x and 1.6x on the A12 (derived from page data); page says wasm3 is fastest on nearly every case it can run.
compiler_and_flags: Harness: pinned nightly-2026-07-05 (1.98.0-nightly, LLVM 22.1.8), fat LTO, 1 codegen unit; Xcode 27.0 Apple clang 21.0.0; wasm32 guests built with Rust 1.93.1. wasm3 v0.9.0 (0cd38327): -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 -std=c99 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions. WAMR cmake Release -O3 -mcpu=apple-a12 INTERP=1 FAST_INTERP=1 AOT=0 JIT=0 FAST_JIT=0. Pulley: RUSTFLAGS=--cfg=pulley_tail_calls -C target-cpu=apple-a12.
tradeoffs: Interpreter only; no SIMD, exceptions, GC, typed function references, memory64 or multi-memory (only tail calls and extended-const of the Wasm 3.0 features); extended-const instantiation costs 116-122x Pulley's time; README announces a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Single small third-party repo (3 stars, about 128 commits; branch names show AI-agent-assisted authorship), not independently replicated. Interpreter-only comparison on Apple Silicon E-cores, built with -mcpu=apple-a12 for both hosts; results may not transfer to x86 or P-cores. Runtimes are patched builds: WAMR is upstream main b70d708d plus 29 patches (relaxed SIMD and legacy EH for fast-interp, PROT_NONE reservation), WasmEdge 0.17.2-rc.3 plus 26 patches built MinSizeRel -Os with WASMEDGE_USE_LLVM=OFF (the author's production-app recipe, which handicaps WasmEdge), Pulley is wasmtime v49.0.0 plus 9 fork commits (table-mutability split, call_indirect arg bundling). Geomean covers only the 17 cases every runtime runs (factorial excluded); wasm3 cannot run SIMD, exceptions, GC, memory64 or multi-memory cases. Cross-language LTO was impossible (Rust nightly LLVM 22 vs Xcode 27 libLTO LLVM 21), so Rust runtimes use fat LTO and C/C++/Zig runtimes link as native objects. Headline tables are CPU time per call (median of 10 reps), results are checked against a cross-runtime consensus so fast wrong answers are errors. Reported here as evidence for a project already in the known list.

name: Silverfir-nano (wasmi-benchmarks 2026 shootout)
baseline: WAMR fast-interpreter and Wasm3 (interpreter mode); V8, Wasmtime Cranelift and Wasmer Cranelift (JIT mode, Apple Silicon only); Wasmtime Winch and Wasmer Singlepass (baseline JITs)
workload: wasmi-benchmarks execute suite (21 test programs: counters, fibonacci, sort, sieve, matrix-mul, nbody, argon2, keccak, mandelbrot, compression, json-parse, regex-redux, bulk-ops and others) summarized as a geomean, plus CoreMark compiled to Wasm; Silverfir-nano run in its interpreter and JIT modes among 23 runtime configurations.
claimed_speedup: Execute geomean (lower is better): interpreter 9.02 on EPYC 7763, 6.30 on M2 Pro, 5.97 on M4 Pro, 5.56 on i7700, 7.01 on Xeon 8573C, against WAMR fast-interpreter 17.07, 14.77, 18.64, 11.11, 12.43 and Wasm3 16.51, 12.64, 10.71, 8.50, 11.95. JIT mode: 1.06 on M2 Pro and 1.07 on M4 Pro versus V8 1.22 and 1.19, Wasmtime Cranelift 1.27 and 1.31, Wasmer Cranelift 1.28 and 1.31 (fastest overall on the two Apple machines); but slower than those three on x86 (EPYC 1.25 vs V8 1.05, Wasmtime Cranelift 1.15, Wasmer Cranelift 1.17; i7700 1.46 vs 1.13, 1.25, 1.24; Xeon 1.28 vs 1.04, 1.21, 1.21). JIT mode beats Wasmtime Winch (2.35 EPYC, 3.12 M2 Pro, 3.17 M4 Pro) and Wasmer Singlepass (2.95, 4.60, 4.85). CoreMark: interpreter 2226 vs WAMR 1286 and Wasm3 1121 on EPYC 7763 (about 1.7x and 2.0x, derived from page data); JIT 37413 on M4 Pro vs Wasmtime Cranelift 38969, Wasmer Cranelift 38434, V8 35334.
compiler_and_flags: wasmi-benchmarks Cargo.toml: [profile.bench] lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1 for the harness and all runtimes; benchmark inputs built from Rust with [profile.wasm] opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort. Runtime pins read from runtimes/*/Cargo.toml: wasmtime 47.0.0, wasmer 7.2.0, v8 crate 150.1.0, wasmi 2.0.0-beta.10 (README links v2.0.0-beta.7), Silverfir-nano git tag 0.5, wasm3 via wasm3x 0.2.1 (Wasm3 v0.9.0), WAMR fast interpreter via wamrx 0.3, stitch from Robbepop/stitch branch v0.1-dev. rustc version not stated (no rust-toolchain file).
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763, Apple M2 Pro, Apple M4 Pro, Intel i7700 (as titled in the plots), Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C (CPU names read from the plot titles and data directories of wasmi-benchmarks-plots; core counts, RAM and OS not stated)
tradeoffs: JIT mode compiles slowly: startup (compile plus instantiate) geomean 926.77 on EPYC versus 33.27 for V8, 298.15 for Wasmtime Winch and 162.12 for Wasmer Singlepass, though faster than the Cranelift engines (1484 to 1634). no_std WebAssembly 3.0 runtime with six native backends (x86_64, ARM64, RV64GC, RV32GC, ARMv7-A, Thumb-2); Rust only, pulled in as a git tag by the suite since it is not on crates.io.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project. The geomean plots report each runtime's time relative to a theoretical optimal runtime (the fastest runtime on every test), so lower is better and 1.00 is optimal; values were read from the rendered SVG plots in wasmi-benchmarks-plots (plots updated 2025-08-25 to 2026-08-27) and CoreMark scores from data/<machine>/coremark.json in wasmi-benchmarks (higher is better; no Xeon 8573C coremark.json, and the Apple M2 Pro file has no JIT rows). The suite is maintained by the Wasmi maintainer (Robbepop), so it is not neutral for Wasmi and the forked Stitch branch. Only the geomean plots were read, not the per-test plots or raw criterion.json. Test inputs are mostly Rust programs compiled to Wasm. The JIT does not beat V8 or the Cranelift engines on the three x86 hosts; its win over them is Apple Silicon only, and by about 11 to 22 percent in the geomean. The project's own RESULTS.md (Apple M4, measured 2026-07-24) also claims parity with Cranelift and the interpreter ahead of wasm3 and wasmi by 1.07 to 1.69x, which is first-party and was not re-derived here. Young project (crate releases aligned at 0.6.0 on 2026-09-09).

The geomean plots report each runtime's time relative to a theoretical optimal runtime (the fastest runtime on every test), so lower is better and 1.00 is optimal; values were read from the rendered SVG plots in wasmi-benchmarks-plots (plots updated 2025-08-25 to 2026-08-27) and CoreMark scores from data/<machine>/coremark.json in wasmi-benchmarks (higher is better; no Xeon 8573C coremark.json, and the Apple M2 Pro file has no JIT rows). Only the geomean plots were read, not the per-test plots or raw criterion.json. Test inputs are mostly Rust programs compiled to Wasm. Silverfir-nano's interpreter is faster than Wasmi 2 on every machine (e.g. 9.02 vs 12.40 on EPYC 7763). The data was collected with 2.0.0-beta builds before the 2.0.0 release on 2026-09-01 (the crate pin reads 2.0.0-beta.10). Wasmi v1 eager starts faster than Wasmi 2 eager on EPYC (25.68 vs 38.88), and lazy-mode rows are not like-for-like with eager rows of other runtimes. A secondary write-up (zeli.app, dated 2026-09-02, snippet only) repeats the project's claim of 2.2x faster than 1.x and ahead of Wasm3, WAMR and Pulley.
